original_query: Why were Eisenhower's two wins relatively weak compared to Harding, Johnson, Nixon, and Reagan? In hindsight at least--perhaps it was different at the time--Eisenhower seems to enjoy a broad degree of respect. Both liberals and conservatives speak fondly of him--as far as high-profile political figures in recent times are concerned, both Bernie Sanders and Donald Trump have done so, for example. And, unlike Dewey, Eisenhower was a non-politician. Dewey was a moderate, but I imagine it's possible he might have been put in a position to make decisions as Governor that could be used against him. Eisenhower, as the commanding general on D-Day, would seem to have commanded a respect akin to Washington or Grant. In 1952, Stevenson himself said, 'Who did I think I was, running against George Washington?' [1] But for all that, Eisenhower got 55.18% of the national popular vote in 1952, and 57.37% in 1956. While impressive, it seems like he had a stubborn floor that was higher than that of several other presidents before and after him, such as Harding, Johnson, Nixon, and, Reagan. The first three of these got over 60% of the vote, and Reagan got 58.77% in 1984. This is despite that all of these seem more controversial and polarising than Eisenhower (and also lacking the supra-political stature of having been a commanding general presiding over something like D-Day). Two things I can think of that might have hurt Eisenhower are 1) Eisenhower's non-denunciation of McCarthy in public, and 2) his running-mate choice (as Nixon had to give a speech defending himself against fraud allegations in 1952). But, whether they would have applied in 1952 or not, they would not seem to have applied in 1956. [1] https://www.americanheritage.com/why-we-were-right-ike

original_query: How frequently is foreign press barred or allowed in war zones? (Yes, this is motivated by the question about press access to Gaza, but don't read support, or criticism, for that question in this one. Merely curiosity about how much we can expect free press access in conflict zones). To give some context of my understanding coming into this question: During the Vietnam War, the US, consciously or not, experimented with press freedom in a war zone. This was largely seen to have been a mistake from the US PoV, whether or not one agreed with war itself . From burning napalm on a child, to a self-immolating monk, to a spot execution of a bound communist sympathizer, a number of instantly-recognizable photos contributed in driving down US domestic support for the war. I kinda recall people stating that that access had been a) unusual and b) mismanaged. With the unusual aspect relevant to my question here. By Gulf War 1, the US had learned its lesson and the press coverage about press coverage was fascinated by the solution found: embedded journalists . Who were vetted, and controlled by, the Pentagon. So, yes, there was access. But, no, it wasn't free access. And, if I recall correctly, no one was much surprised or outraged, just a bit cynical about the press freedom quotient to be expected. In the Ukraine war, the press does have access to the Ukraine side of things. But even people highly sympathetic to Ukraine can understand that Ukraine has a vested interest in presenting its plight on the world stage. Free press access is of benefit to Ukraine, which is not doubt a huge part of the reasons it is allowed. On the Russian side of things, no, I don't think there is free access to foreign journalists to the occupied regions. They do conduct tours , of sorts, mostly with picked Western "journalists" of dubious quality. India has found it expedient at times to bar foreign press in Kashmir for months at a time. RSF in 2020 : "The Kashmir Valley, from which foreign reporters had already been barred for several months" Yes, there are plenty of counterinsurgency conflicts - presumably what Gaza is supposed to be at this point - where press is allowed, under various levels of control, by the official government. But in many cases, the "coverage of the coverage" also points out the reason: the government wants to appear strong and in control and a press blackout would give the opposite impression. Keep that in mind when looking at historical access to Gaza - just because it was allowed at one time doesn't mean the same calculation about the cost/benefit applies nowadays, from the Israeli side. Yes, at times Israel has allowed foreign press into Gaza, under highly controlled conditions, for example to show tunnels under hospitals. This is akin to Gulf War 1 embedded reporters and isn't generally seen as free press access. Guerrillas, rebels and sometimes even terrorists often explicitly covet coverage, consider press access a tool in their struggle and therefore allow it. But, like Ukraine, one should be under no illusion about why this is allowed, regardless of where one's sympathy lies. So, on balance is foreign press access the norm, or the exception, in conflict zones, on the government side? Especially by democracies, rather than authoritarian regimes. p.s. At the risk of stating the obvious, the press itself will almost always insist on press freedom. This question isn't about what the press thinks, nor whether public opinion thinks that the press should be allowed or not. It is concerned with what is normative/customary with regards to foreign press access in war zones. p.p.s. Be cautious about survivor bias here. Merely citing all the conflict coverage you can recall doesn't tell us much about the cases where it wasn't allowed. p.p.p.s. It was already in the comments, but it seems to have been missed: while it is motivated by the Gaza situation this question is explicitly not about Gaza : we already know the foreign press is barred there.

original_query: Why are special pensions still needed in a modern capitalist state? Context In Romania, there was much debate related to the "fairness" of special pensions, and this rather lengthy EU Commission document confirms this: Currently, eight special pension schemes are in place in Romania. They are for: 1) military personnel, police and national security system personnel, 2) magistrates, 3) specialised auxiliary personnel from the courts and prosecutor's offices, 4) workers in civil aeronautics, 5) parliamentary civil servants, 6) Court of Accounts personnel, 7) diplomats, and 8) deputies and senators. In addition, a new scheme addressing officials at local and county level (i.e. mayors, deputy mayors, presidents and deputy presidents of county councils) is expected to enter into force in 2021 (GO57/2019, GO 1/2020). The new law aims to scrap all special schemes and subsequently to integrate them into the main PAYG scheme, with the exception of pensions for military and police personnel. This makes me wonder why the concept of a special pension still exists. By special pension I mean retirement benefits not linked to social security contributions, often granted to certain public officials or specific groups under unique legal provisions. Details I understand that some jobs cannot be done until in your 60s (e.g. chasing criminals in the street, fighting in the front line). So, the general pension scheme cannot work for everybody, but the general pension scheme could be used with some tweaks. Examples: salaries could be raised enough for the people to be interested in that job, just like for the other jobs one year of work could gain more years towards the retirement threshold. Example (actually implemented where I live): anyone working in a dangerous environment such as mines, working with explosive substances etc. could get as much as 150% - 200% years towards the retirement threshold. Why are special pensions still needed in a modern capitalist state?

original_query: What's the nature of HMO (health maintenance organizations) involvement with Medicare, if any? Medicare is the US's universal coverage for over 65s (not to be confused with Medicaid, for those too poor to afford insurance). HMOs are a type of medical insurers particular to the US system. The motivation for asking this question is that the US has a very expensive overall system for delivering health care. And, of course, if it was ever to be reformed the resulting savings - to consumers and to the government - would mean direct losses for some of the actors that benefit from those inefficiencies. Which means that they are incentivized to lobby energetically to avoid reforms. There are a number of cost drivers in health care: medicine: pharmaceutical companies, pharmacies and middlemen care delivery: hospitals, staff malpractice insurance health insurance: insurance providers, notably HMOs - Health Maintenance Organizations ) , which were originally intended as a cost-saving mechanism . HMOs - not supplemental health insurers - are a uniquely American, some would say uniquely rapacious, factor in health care. Some of those HMOs have just become giant profit centers instead and have every incentive to be involved in as many medical transactions as possible. Unlike the other components of health care, which can be rationalized and reformed but still need to be delivered to patients, HMOs don't seem to have a real reason for existence, in terms of patient outcomes or health provisioning. Which means that transitioning to a single payer system is anathema to them. Single-payer health care is a system in which the government, rather than private insurers, pays for all health care costs.[48] Single-payer systems may contract for healthcare services from private organizations, or own and employ healthcare resources and personnel... Yet, the US has a single payer system (I think), in the form of Medicare. And Medicare, due to attending to older people, means a lot of medical treatment, and thus lots of $$$, issuing from the government. Are the HMOs set up to capture any of that money, aside from voluntary supplemental coverage that consumers may wish to purchase? Or are they cut out entirely? This was motivated by a recently closed question about gradually transitioning US health care - one mechanism could be to gradually decrease the Medicare threshold from 65 over time. Which got me to wonder what involvement, if any, HMOs have with the biggest spigot of Federal health care dollars, Medicare.

original_query: Why does South Korea's presidential impeachment process involve the judiciary? The BBC reports that the South Korean Parliament has voted to impeach Han Duck-Soo , the current acting president of South Korea. It also reported that the impeachment will only happen if the South Korean constitutional court also upholds it: BBC (27 December 2024) : South Korea has voted to impeach its acting president Han Duck-soo, two weeks after parliament voted to impeach its President Yoon Suk Yeol ... Korea's Constitutional Court is typically made up of a nine-member bench. At least six judges must uphold Yoon's impeachment in order for the decision to be upheld. There are currently only six judges on the bench, meaning a single rejection would save Yoon from being removed. The Guardian has also reported that the trial of the former president Yoon Suk Yeol , for his impeachment, is also set to begin on 27 December 2024: South Korean president Yoon Suk Yeol’s legal team are set to attend court on Friday as the constitutional court begins hearings into his impeachment by parliament over his short-lived imposition of martial law ... The court has 180 days to decide whether to reinstate Yoon or remove him. In the latter scenario, a new presidential election would be held within 60 days. The Wikipedia page on the Constitutional Court of Korea states: For passage, the [impeachment] motion must receive the support of a two-thirds majority if it concerns the president and a simple majority for any other office. Once the impeachment motion passes the National Assembly, the Constitutional Court adjudicates the impeachment, and until the Constitutional Court renders a decision, the impeached official is suspended from office and unable to exercise power. Involving the judiciary in a political process seems contrary to the doctrine of separation of powers in a democracy. As far as I am aware, most mature democracies tend to limit the scope of judicial review of normal legislative activities. Impeachment process, deemed to be a political process , thus also falls in the exclusive domain of the Legislature (i.e. the elected representatives are deemed to be the competent authority to adjudicate on such matters; criminal proceedings against the impeached official, if necessary, tend to be filed separately, and are often independent of the impeachment process.) So, why does the South Korean impeachment process involve both the Legislature and the Judiciary ?

Estonia has used internet voting (" I-voting ") since 2005, with over 50% of voters casting their ballots online in the most recent election . It remains the only democracy in the world where the majority of voters are eligible to vote online. Additionally, Russia plans to implement it nationwide by 2026 , although critics argue the primary motivation is electoral fraud rather than an effort to increase voter participation. Given Estonia's nearly flawless track record over two decades, why are other countries still hesitant to adopt a similar system and simplify voting for their citizens? Prior research The most comprehensive criticism of e-voting was published by Springall et al. in 2014. It outlined several issues with the system and ended with the following recommendation: After studying other e-voting systems around the world, the team was particularly alarmed by the Estonian I-voting system. It has serious design weaknesses that are exacerbated by weak operational management. It has been built on assumptions which are outdated and do not reflect the contemporary reality of state-level attacks and sophisticated cybercrime. These problems stem from fundamental architectural problems that cannot be resolved with quick fixes or interim steps. While we believe e-government has many promising uses, the Estonian I-voting system carries grave risks — elections could be stolen, disrupted, or cast into disrepute. In light of these problems, our urgent recommendation is that to maintain the integrity of the Estonian electoral process, use of the Estonian I-voting system should be immediately discontinued. However, from what I understand, many of the issues identified were addressed by 2021 , and large portions of the online voting system were published as open-source for the sake of transparency. It is difficult for me to gauge the remaining risks, but Estonia continues using the system, and it seems to be functioning well for them so far.

AP, October 29, 2024 One of the bills passed Monday evening bans all UNRWA activities and services on Israeli soil and is set to take effect in three months. The second bill severs all ties between government employees and UNRWA and strips its staff of their legal immunities. Together, the bills likely bar the agency from operating in Israel and the Palestinian territories, because Israel controls access to both Gaza and the West Bank. It could force the agency to relocate its headquarters from Israeli-annexed east Jerusalem. The agency is the major distributor of aid in Gaza and provides education , health and other basic services to millions of Palestinian refugees across the region, including in the Israeli-occupied West Bank. Note: this question is strictly limited to education. (This question is concerned with the future after a ceasefire. Running schools is not that realistic right now.) In the past, Israel has indicated strong disquiet with the format of education, under UNRWA, to Palestinians , claiming that schoolbooks encourage hatred of Israelis. Now, Israel seems to understand that something needs to take over from UNRWA : "UNRWA workers involved in terrorist activities against Israel must be held accountable," the office of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on social media hours after the Knesset vote. "Since avoiding a humanitarian crisis is also essential, sustained humanitarian aid must remain available in Gaza now and in the future. In the 90 days before this legislation takes effect — and after — we stand ready to work with our international partners to ensure Israel continues to facilitate humanitarian aid to civilians in Gaza in a way that does not threaten Israel's security. How will education be provided in the future? Education is not like food, or medicine. It can't just handed over at the border. Those alleged (but likely) inflammatory teachings in books and classroom speech were - allegedly - provided by UNRWA, a theoretically neutral UN agency. They in turn claim a lot of their alleged anti-Israel bias was imposed by Hamas, as a cost of "doing business" in Gaza. What is going to replace UNRWA schooling then? Anything run more directly by the locals is likely to be even more critical of Israel. Even a thorough editorial review/censorship of school books being used won't stop teachers from verbal indoctrination, should they choose to. And putting pro-Israel, or at least really neutral, teachers or supervisors in the schools (either locals or "international partners") would put those people in great danger under the foreseeable circumstances (i.e. a ceasefire, but no durable peace, in Gaza). What's the Israeli plan then? What's going to ensure neutrality at the point of delivery, since that was the issue in the first place, education-wise. p.s. No, this question is not about funding . It is about Israeli plans to fix the UNRWA's alleged bias, while still providing education. p.p.s. (in response to a comment about secrecy) These laws were passed in the Knesset and I assume arrangements for providing replacement services were debated there, under no seal of secrecy.
